findings.detail: D5 [C2 weaknesses[1]; practicalImplications; furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion] The severity of the residual impact (41s, about 6% of sessions erroring) is not tied to any availability target or error budget. The draft lists 'may breach SLOs' as a weakness but does not name finding the SLO as a verification step. Without it, the priority of the retry fix and failover tuning cannot be judged.

D1 [criteriaAssessments C6 assessment and strengths[1]; mechanisms ('as this request shows')] C6 says the request is 'evidence the stale page is already causing wrong decisions'. That overstates it. The request is a question about prioritisation, and no wrong decision has been made yet. The supportable claim is that the stale page nearly misdirected planning. This also slightly inflates the case for doc work under C6.

D2 [criteriaAssessments C3 assessment] C3 calls the 41s failover window 'an equally plausible contributor' to the INC-2291 errors. The packet has no basis for weighting the two causes equally. The source records only that the retry item is an open action item, and E7 is snippet-level. 'Also plausible' is supportable; 'equally' is not.

D4 [alternatives; tradeoffs[2]; practicalImplications[3]] For the residual whole-cluster mass-logout risk (C4), the draft considers only server-side durability (persistence or snapshots). It leaves out the application-side alternative: making session loss graceful through re-authentication, refresh tokens, or a fallback session source. That could be cheaper than enabling and operating persistence, and it is relevant to C5's cost comparison.

D3 [CL7, K4, C2 assessment] K4 and CL7 compute a ratio (0.18) and then say it 'says nothing reliable about client behaviour'. A calculation the draft itself calls uninformative adds noise and false precision without informing the decision. Either drop it or state what it would take to make it informative (for example, the share of sessions active during the 41s window).
